The Pacific Plate moves northwest relative to the North American Plate at about 5 cm/yr. The Nazca Plate subducts, meaning it sinks beneath another plate, under South America at about 8 cm/yr. Postseismic — afterslip and viscoelastic relaxation move stress around (months to years) 4. Preseismic — possible warning signals: foreshocks, slow slip
Restated in other words: between quakes, strain builds slowly over long periods; the quake itself releases it in moments; afterwards, stress is redistributed over months to years; and warning signals may appear before the next one. ## Earthquake Depth Distribution
Earthquakes do not occur at one single depth. Their depth depends on the plate setting, which is the type of boundary where plates meet. This matters because depth and plate speed control where large earthquakes happen often, and this knowledge is used directly in hazard assessment, the work of judging future earthquake risk. Try first: before reading further, write down from memory which depth range you expect at a divergent ridge, and which you expect at a subducting slab. Type your answer. The worked material follows.
Depth by setting, in words: shallow events, at 10 km depth or less, dominate divergent ridges and transform faults. Intermediate to deep events, from 30 to 300 km, occur in the Wadati-Benioff zone. The Wadati-Benioff zone is the zone inside a sinking slab where earthquakes form. A subducting slab is a plate that bends and sinks beneath another plate. The same idea as a picture in text: Setting Depth range Divergent ridge → shallow (≤ 10 km) Transform fault → shallow (≤ 10 km) Subducting slab (Wadati-Benioff zone) → 30–300 km

Worked step: a typical subduction earthquake at 30 km depth releases energy from two sources. First, crustal bending, meaning the slab bends as it sinks. Second, slab dehydration. Dehydration means water is driven out of the slab as it sinks and heats up. Both processes free energy at depth.
Think of it like a k-pop dance formation: the front row, which stands for shallow ridges and transforms, moves constantly, while the deep layers of the formation, which stand for the sinking slab, move only when the whole shape bends. The bending and the release of water are what free energy at depth. The analogy maps to the two energy sources named above; it adds no new fact about earthquakes. Restated in different words: at shallow boundaries earthquakes are frequent and near the surface; at depth, energy is freed only when the slab bends and loses its water. The lithosphere is Earth's rigid outer layer. It is broken into a mosaic of rigid tectonic plates.
These plates float on the asthenosphere. That is a ductile layer, meaning it can slowly flow.
